## 1. Introduction

In 1936, Cramér introduced a probabilistic model for predicting features of the primes. In this model, $\mathbbm{1}_{n\text{ is prime}}$ is modeled by a random variable $X_{n}$ with $\mathbb{P}(X_{n}=1)=1-\mathbb{P}(X_{n}=0)=1/\log n$ . We have that almost surely

$$ \lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{n\leqslant X}X_{n}}{\sum_{n\leqslant X}\mathbbm{1}_{n\text{ prime}}}=1. $$

In particular, Cramér’s model matches the Prime Number Theorem. It is interesting to test Cramér’s heuristic as a method for modeling finer aspects of the distribution of the primes. Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, it is known that Cramér’s model matches the truth for primes in intervals of the shape $[X,X+X^{1/2+\varepsilon}]$ . For $\lambda>2$ , Cramér’s model suggests that

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+(\log X)^{\lambda}}\mathbbm{1}_{n\text{ is prime}}=(1+o(1))\frac{(\log X)^{\lambda}}{\log X} $$

since

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+(\log X)^{\lambda}}X_{n}=(1+o(1))\frac{(\log X)^{\lambda}}{\log X} $$

almost surely. It turns out that the naive conjecture described above is false, and

#### Theorem 1.1 (Maier, [15]).

Fix $\lambda>1$ and set $H=(\log X)^{\lambda}$ . Then, the following holds:

$$ \limsup_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\pi(X+H)-\pi(X)}{H/\log X}>1, $$

and

$$ \liminf_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\pi(X+H)-\pi(X)}{H/\log X}<1. $$

Following Maier’s remarkable result, similar results on the inequidistribution of other arithmetic sequences in short intervals were obtained by Balog-Wooley [1] on numbers representable as sums of two squares, and Tongsomporn and Steuding [24] on primes in Beatty sequences. Later, Maynard [20] combined Maier’s methods with sieve theory to push these results further for prime numbers and numbers representable as the sum of two squares. Additionally, Thorne [23] has shown the function field analogue of Theorem 1.1.

Granville and Soundararajan [8] generalized Maier’s work and showed that a more general class of arithmetic sequences will be poorly distributed in either short intervals or short arithmetic progressions. In particular, they demonstrated that this phenomenon is not specific to the primes.

Friedlander and Granville [5] use Maier’s method show the analogue of Maier’s result for short arithmetic progressions. Specifically, writing $\pi(X,q,a)=\#\{p\leqslant X:p\equiv a\mod q,p\text{ prime}\}$ , it is shown that for fixed $A>2$ , large $X$ there exists $q_{\pm}\in[X,2X]$ such that

$$ \pi(X(\log X)^{A},q_{+},1)>(1+\delta_{A})\frac{X}{\varphi(q_{+})(\log X)^{A-1}}, $$

$$ \pi(X(\log X)^{A},q_{-},1)<(1-\delta_{A})\frac{X}{\varphi(q_{-})(\log X)^{A-1}}. $$

There has been further work on these lines by Friedlander, Granville, Hildebrand, and Maier [6].

Before we state our general result, we shall discuss some special cases of our main theorem. In [25], Vinogradov shows for odd $N$ that

$$ \#\{p_{1},p_{2},p_{3}\in[0,N]:p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3}=N\}=\frac{\mathfrak{S}(N)}{2}\frac{N^{2}}{(\log N)^{3}}, $$

where

$$ \mathfrak{S}(N)=\prod_{p|N}\bigg(1-\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\bigg)\prod_{p\nmid N}\bigg(1+\frac{1}{(p-1)^{3}}\bigg). $$

One might desire to understand the distribution of pairs $(n_{1},n_{2})$ for which $n_{1},n_{2},N-n_{1}-n_{2}$ are all prime. By the above result, an analogue of Cramér’s model might be to model $\mathbbm{1}_{n_{1},n_{2},N-n_{1}-n_{2}\text{ prime}}$ by a random variable $X_{n_{1},n_{2}}$ with

$$ \mathbb{P}(X_{n_{1},n_{2}}=1)=1-\mathbb{P}(X_{n_{1},n_{2}}=0)=\frac{\mathfrak{S}(N)}{2(\log N)^{3}} $$

Unconditionally, Zhan [26] has an asymptotic the count of $(n_{1},n_{2})$ such that $n_{1},n_{2},$ and $N-n_{1}-n_{2}$ are prime, and that the $n_{i}$ are restricted to appropriate short intervals of length at least $N^{\frac{5}{8}}(\log N)^{c}$ for some $c>0$ . This analogue of Cramér’s model would suggest that one would be able to count such $n_{i}$ in short intervals as short as $(\log X)^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda>2$ .

A special case of our main theorem provides an answer in the negative to the this Cramér-type model provides. Specifically, we show:

#### Corollary 1.2.

Let $N$ be a sufficiently large odd number and $\lambda>\frac{3}{2}$ . Let $N\ll X\leqslant N/6,H=(\log X)^{\lambda}$ . There exist $\delta_{\lambda}^{+},\delta_{\lambda}^{-}>0$ such that for $X$ sufficiently large, there exist $x^{\pm},y^{\pm}\in[X,2X]$ such that

$$ \#\{p_{1}\in[x^{+},x^{+}+H],p_{2}\in[y^{+},y^{+}+H]:N-p_{1}-p_{2}\textrm{ prime}\}\geqslant(1+\delta_{\lambda}^{+})\mathfrak{S}(N)\frac{H^{2}}{(\log X)^{3}}, $$

$$ \#\{p_{1}\in[x^{-},x^{-}+H],p_{2}\in[y^{-},y^{-}+H]:N-p_{1}-p_{2}\textrm{ prime}\}\leqslant(1-\delta_{\lambda}^{-})\mathfrak{S}(N)\frac{H^{2}}{(\log X)^{3}}. $$

This result can be shown using a combination of Maier’s matrix method and the circle method. Our main theorem, however, can be applied to a broader class of equations that are beyond the reach of the circle method. For instance, we can instead consider primes in four term arithmetic progressions, and show similar irregularities in the distribution of $(x,y)$ such that $x,x+y,x+2y,x+3y$ are all prime.

Next, we introduce the general setting. Let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{t}):\mathbb{Z}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a system of linear forms.

#### Definition 1.

The complexity of a system of forms $\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{t})$ is the smallest integer $s\geqslant 0$ such that $\{\tilde{\psi_{j}}:[t]\backslash\{i\}\}$ can be partitioned into $s+1$ classes such that $\tilde{\psi_{i}}$ is not contained in the affine linear span of any of the classes, where $\tilde{\psi}$ denotes the homogeneous part of $\psi$ .

We will restrict ourselves to systems of finite complexity, which measures the linear independence of the homogeneous parts of the forms. In [9], Green and Tao show that a system has finite complexity if and only if the $\tilde{\psi_{i}}$ are pairwise pairwise linearly independent. In particular, twin primes and Goldbach’s conjecture both have infinite complexity; as a result, we are not able to say anything about such primes using this technology.

In their seminal work, Green and Tao proved the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture for linear patterns with finite complexity. Let us take $\Lambda(n)=\Lambda(|n|)$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus{\left\{0\right\}}$ and $\Lambda(0)=0$ .

#### Theorem 1.3 (Green and Tao, [9]).

Let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},...,\psi_{t})$ be a system of finite complexity. Then the following asymptotic holds:

$$ \sum_{\textbf{x}\in[-X,X]^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\textbf{x}))=(2X)^{d}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}+o_{\Psi}(X^{d}), $$

where

$$ \beta_{p}=p^{-d}\sum_{\textbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\left(\frac{p}{p-1}\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(\textbf{x}),p)=1}\right). $$

We note that this asymptotic is not exactly what Cramér’s model predicts, but is properly corrected by the local factors $\beta_{p}$ for the system $\Psi$ . A random model for the primes along the lines of Cramér, correcting for these local factors was found by Granville [7]. In [17], Matomäki, Shao, Tao and Teräväinen, have confirmed that the asymptotic holds in short boxes of length $H\geqslant X^{5/8+\varepsilon}$ :

#### Theorem 1.4 (Matomäki, Shao, Tao, and Teräväinen, [17]).

Let $X^{5/8+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ . Let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},...,\psi_{t}):\mathbb{Z}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ have finite complexity. Then we have that

$$ \sum_{\textbf{x}\in[X,X+H]^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\textbf{x}))=H^{d}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}+o_{\Psi}(H^{d}). $$

We study the limits to equidistribution with the following result.

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $\lambda>1$ , $X$ sufficiently large, and $H=(\log X)^{\lambda}$ . Then, there exist $\delta_{\lambda}^{+},\delta_{\lambda}^{-}>0$ such that there exists $\textbf{x}^{\pm}\in[X,2X]^{d}$ such that

$$ \sum_{\textbf{x}\in\prod_{i=1}^{d}[x^{+}_{i},x^{+}_{i}+H]}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{\psi_{i}(\textbf{x})\textrm{ is prime}}\geqslant(1+\delta_{\lambda}^{+})\frac{H^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}, $$

and

$$ \sum_{\textbf{x}\in\prod_{i=1}^{d}[x^{-}_{i},x^{-}_{i}+H]}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{\psi_{i}(\textbf{x})\textrm{ is prime}}\leqslant(1-\delta_{\lambda}^{-})\frac{H^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}. $$

#### Remark 1.

We note that we expect primes in these patterns to be equidistributed in large enough boxes because it is a linear system. If instead we look at quadratic polynomials, then there are large cone regions where there are no integer solutions. For example, there are no primes of the form $m^{2}+n^{2}$ for $0<m,n\leqslant X$ with $0<\arg(m+ni)<\frac{1}{X}$ , for there are no integral points in the region. However, equidistribution would predict in most sectors of angle $\asymp\frac{1}{X}$ , there are $\asymp\frac{X}{\log X}$ primes.

These irregularities are due to the structure of the lattice points for the quadratic in certain sectors. In our linear case, there are no such obstructions to regularity; the number of lattice points in $\prod_{i}[x_{i},x_{i}+H]$ remains $(1+o(1))H^{d}$ for all $x_{i}$ . Thus, the relative abundance or sparsity of linear patterns of primes is therefore due to the structure of the primes and not immediately due to the fact that they sit inside the integers.

#### Remark 2.

We expect to be able to show the analogue of our result in short arithmetic progressions rather than short intervals à la Friedlander and Granville [5].

#### Remark 3.

For a fixed $\lambda$ and a range $[X,2X]^{d}$ , we note that if worked out, we can get $\delta_{\lambda}^{\pm}$ to grow exponentially with $t$ . In particular, as $t$ grows, we get counts in small boxes that deviate by an arbitrarily large constant factor from the expected count. We are thus able to find deviations that are in a sense more severe than those of Maier.

We end this section with a brief outline of the rest of the paper. In §2, we will set up the main results from which our main theorem follows; in §2.3 we complete the proof of Theorem 1.5 assuming these two results, to whose proofs the rest of the paper will be devoted. In §3, we set up the machinery surrounding nilsequences we shall require in our proof . What remains is then reduced to certain estimates sums of nilsequences along primes in arithmetic progressions with moderately large moduli, which we show in §4; it is here where new ideas are brought in.

## 2. Setup

### 2.1. Notation

In this section, we will specify notation that will be used for the remainder of the paper. We fix a system of form $\Psi=(\psi_{1},...,\psi_{t}):\mathbb{Z}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ of finite complexity $s$ . We write $[N]=\{1,2,...,N\}.$ Associated to these forms are the local densities $\beta_{p}$ , as defined in Theorem 1.3.

Throughout, $p$ always denotes a prime. Write $P(z)=\prod_{p\leqslant z}p$ . We will use $\mathcal{P}$ to denote the set of prime numbers.

We let $\omega:\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 1}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 1}$ be the Buchstab function, i.e. the unique continuous function such that

$$ \displaystyle\omega(u) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{u},\hskip 7.0pt1\leqslant u\leqslant 2 \displaystyle\frac{d}{du}(u\omega(u)) \displaystyle=\omega(u-1),\hskip 7.0ptu\geqslant 2 $$

Throughout, $\gamma$ shall denote the Euler-Mascheroni constant.

### 2.2. Existence of dutiful moduli

#### Definition 2.

A modulus $Q$ is dutiful if for all $q\leqslant(\log Q)^{\frac{1}{10}}$ , all of the Dirichlet characters $\chi\mod{(qQ)^{{\left\lfloor 20s\log\log Q\right\rfloor}}}$ satisfy that for any $\beta\in[1/2,1]$ such that $L(\beta,\chi)=0$ , the following holds:

$$ \beta\leqslant 1-\frac{1}{(\log Q)^{2}}. $$

#### Remark 4.

We note that the choice of $1/10$ here is somewhat arbitrary. It is chosen for notational simplicity and to simply have fewer variables to keep track of through the proof.

#### Proposition 2.1.

There arbitrarily large $z$ such that $P(z)$ is a dutiful modulus.

#### Proof.

We proceed similarly to the proof of Lemma 1 in [14]. Write

$$ M(z)=(P(z)({\lceil\log^{1/10}P(z)\rceil}!))^{{\left\lfloor 20s\log\log P(z)\right\rfloor}}. $$

We record $\log M(z)=(1+o(1))20sz\log z$ . Take some $z_{1}$ sufficiently large. If $P(z_{1})$ is dutiful, we are done. Otherwise (since $z$ is sufficiently large and $\log M(z)=o(\log^{2}P(z))$ ), there exists some $\tilde{\chi}\mod M(z_{1})$ with $L(\tilde{\beta},\tilde{\chi})=0$ and

$$ 1-\tilde{\beta}\leqslant\frac{c_{1}}{\log M(z_{1})} $$

for some sufficiently small $c_{1}$ . Since $z$ is sufficiently large and $\log M(z)=(1+o(1))20sz\log z$ , there exists $z\geqslant z_{1}$ such that

$$ \frac{c_{1}/2}{\log M(z)}<1-\tilde{\beta}\leqslant\frac{c_{1}}{\log M(z)} $$

Therefore, $\tilde{\chi}$ induced $\mod M(z)$ is still an exceptional character to modulus $M(z)$ .

It follows by Theorem 5.28 in [13] (Landau/Page’s theorem) that there are no other exceptional characters $\mod M(z)$ So, for all $\chi\mod M(z)$ , we have that if

$$ 1-\beta\leqslant\frac{c_{1}/2}{\log M(z)}, $$

then $L(\beta,\chi)\neq 0.$ The desired result then follows upon noting that for large $z$ ,

$$ \frac{c_{1}/2}{\log M(z)}\geqslant\frac{1}{(\log P(z))^{2}}. $$

∎

### 2.3. Main estimates

To prove Therorem 1.5, we shall rely on the following two propositions, from which we shall prove the Theorem 1.5 in the next subsection.

#### Definition 3.

For a given modulus $Q$ , $\textbf{a}\in(\mathbb{Z}/Q\mathbb{Z})^{d}$ is called admissible if

$(\psi_{i}(\textbf{a}),Q)=1$ for all $i\leqslant t$ .

#### Proposition 2.2.

Suppose that $Q=P(z)$ is dutiful, and fix $\varepsilon>0$ . Then, for $X\geqslant\exp((\log Q)^{50})$ , admissible $\textbf{a}\in(\mathbb{Z}/Q\mathbb{Z})^{d}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
{\bf n\equiv\bf a}(Q)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(n))=\frac{1}{\#\mathcal{A}}\frac{X^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}(1+O(z^{-1}))+o{\left(\frac{X^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\right)}. $$

Here, $\mathcal{A}\subset(\mathbb{Z}/Q\mathbb{Z})^{d}$ is the set of admissible tuples $\mod Q$ .

We remark that for almost all $Q\leqslant X^{\frac{1}{3}-\varepsilon}$ , Teräväinen and Shao [21] have shown Proposition 2.2.

We also introduce an estimate for linear patterns of rough numbers. This result follows from general work of Matthiessen [19, Theorem 2.1], though in our specific case of rough numbers, we expect that it should also follow with a little work from results on linear patterns of primes.

#### Proposition 2.3.

Fix $u>1$ , take $z$ large, and let $N=z^{u}$ . Then, we have

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf n}\in[N,2N]^{d}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(n),P(z))=1}=(1+o(1))\frac{\#\mathcal{A}}{P(z)^{d}}\left(e^{\gamma}\omega(u)\right)^{t}N^{d}, $$

where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of admissible tuples $\mod P(z)$ .

#### Proof.

We note that $\mathbbm{1}_{(.,P(z))=1}$ is a multiplicative function. Let us take on the notation of [19]; we note that $\mathbbm{1}_{(.,P(z))=1}$ satisfies the all of the conditions to apply Theorem 2.1 except condition (iii). However, this issue is only an obstacle in the proof that the constructed measure is pseudorandom. However, since $\mathbbm{1}_{(.,P(z))}\leqslant\mathbbm{1}_{\text{prime}}$ , we can use the pseudorandom measure defined by Green and Tao in [9] and proceed with the proof of Theorem 2.1 in [19].

Take $\tilde{W}(x)=\prod_{p\leqslant\log\log N}p$ . Then, Theorem 2.1 in [19] gives us that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf n}\in[N,2N]^{d}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(n),P(z))=1}\\
=(1+o(1))\frac{\omega(u)^{t}}{(\log z)^{t}}\sum_{(A_{i},\tilde{W})=1}\frac{\tilde{W}^{t}}{\tilde{W}^{d}\varphi(\tilde{W})^{t}}\sum_{v\in\mathbb{Z}/\tilde{W}\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{\psi_{i}(v)\equiv A_{i}\mod\tilde{W}} $$

Now let us take $B>0$ large; for $1\leqslant w_{i}\leqslant(\log N)^{B}$ , if both $\mathbbm{1}_{(w_{i},P(z))=1}\neq 0$ and $p\mid w_{i}\implies p\mid\tilde{W}$ , then $w_{i}=1$ . So the sum over $w_{i}$ ’s becomes

$$ (1+o(1))\frac{\omega(u)^{t}}{(\log z)^{t}}\sum_{(A_{i},\tilde{W})=1}\frac{\tilde{W}^{t}}{\tilde{W}^{d}\varphi(\tilde{W})^{t}}\sum_{v\in\mathbb{Z}/\tilde{W}\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{\psi_{i}(v)\equiv A_{i}\mod\tilde{W}}\\
=(1+o(1))\frac{\omega(u)^{t}}{(\log z)^{t}}\cdot\prod_{p\leqslant\log\log N}\beta_{p}. $$

Now, we can see that

$$ \prod_{p\leqslant\log\log(N)}\beta_{p}=\frac{\#{\mathcal{A}}}{P(z)^{d}}\cdot\frac{P(z)^{t}}{\varphi(P(z))^{t}}\cdot(1+O(z^{-1}+(\log\log N)^{-1}), $$

as both sides can be related to $\prod_{p}\beta_{p}$ . Finally,

$$ \frac{P(z)}{\varphi(P(z))}=\prod_{p\leqslant z}(1-1/p)^{-1}\sim e^{\gamma}(\log z), $$

as desired. ∎

### 2.4. Proof of main theorem

We now prove the main theorem using Maier’s matrix method, assuming Propositions 2.2 and 2.3.

Take $Q=P(z)$ a sufficiently large dutiful modulus, and let

$$ X=Q{\lfloor\exp((\log Q)^{100})/Q\rfloor} $$

so that $Q|X$ . Next, take $U=z^{u}$ , for some $u$ to be determined later. As in the Maier matrix method, we shall estimate the following sum

$$ \Sigma=\sum_{\textbf{a}\in[U,2U]^{d}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
\textbf{n}\equiv\textbf{a}(Q)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\bf n)). $$

in two different ways.

On one hand, we note that the inner sum only contributes if a is admissible. Then, we may estimate the inner sum with Proposition 2.2, and then execute the second sum in the second line with Proposition 2.3. By this, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{a}\in[U,2U]^{d}\\
\textbf{a}\text{ admissible}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
\textbf{n}\equiv\textbf{a}(Q)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n})) \displaystyle=(1+o(1))\frac{X^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\cdot\prod_{p}\beta_{p}\cdot\frac{1}{\#\mathcal{A}}\sum_{\textbf{a}\in[U,2U]^{d}}\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(\textbf{a}),Q)=1\forall i} \displaystyle=(1+o(1))\frac{U^{d}X^{d}}{Q^{d}(\log X)^{t}}\cdot(e^{\gamma}\omega(u))^{t}\cdot\prod_{p}\beta_{p}. $$

On the other hand, rearranging, we have

$$ \Sigma=\sum_{\mathbf{r}\in[(X-U)/Q,2(X-U)/Q]^{d}}\sum_{\textbf{n}\in R_{\mathbf{r}}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n})), $$

where

$$ R_{\mathbf{r}}=\prod_{j\leqslant d}[Q\mathbf{r}_{j}+U,Q\mathbf{r}_{j}+2U]. $$

Since $\Sigma$ is the average over all $\mathbf{r}\in[(X-U)/Q,2(X-U)/Q]^{d}$ , there must exist $\mathbf{r}^{\pm}\in[(X-U)/Q,2(X-U)/Q]^{d}$ such that

$$ \sum_{\textbf{n}\in R_{\mathbf{r}^{+}}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n}))\geqslant(1+o(1))(e^{\gamma}\omega(u))^{t}U^{d}(\log X)^{-t}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}, $$

$$ \sum_{\textbf{n}\in R_{\mathbf{r}^{-}}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n}))\leqslant(1+o(1))(e^{\gamma}\omega(u))^{t}U^{d}(\log X)^{-t}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}. $$

The desired result follows from the fact that for any $u$ , there exist $u^{+},u^{-}\geqslant u$ such that $e^{\gamma}\omega(u^{-})<1<e^{\gamma}\omega(u^{+})$ (see Lemma 4 in [15], for example). Finally, let us take $u=101\lambda$ so that $z^{u}\geqslant(\log X)^{\lambda}$ . Let us look at the short boxes of length $U^{+}=z^{u^{+}}$ (resp. $U^{-}=z^{u^{-}}$ ); applying the pigeonhole within the box, we can see that there is a box of length $(\log X)^{\lambda}$ with an exceptionally large (resp. small) number of primes.

#### Remark 5.

We remark that it is not necessary to take $Q=P(z)$ in these arguments; more generally we could take $Q=\prod_{p\in\mathcal{S}}p$ for $\mathcal{S}$ a subset of the primes that grows with $z$ .

## 3. The Green-Tao Machinery

Let $f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be an arithmetic function, and let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{t}):\mathbb{Z}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{t}$ be a system of linear forms with complexity $s$ . Assume that

$$ \mathbb{E}f(n)=\delta+o(1) $$

for some constant $\delta>0$ . Consider the following sum:

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{R}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f(\psi_{i}(\mathbf{r})). $$

The method of Green and Tao in [9] allows us to find asymptotics for the above sum, assuming “nice” properties of $f$ . We later will take $f$ so that we may count either primes or rough numbers. In either scenario, we must assume that $f$ is bounded by a “constant-like” function — a pseudorandom measure.

#### Definition 4.

A $k$ -pseudorandom measure $\nu:[N]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a function that satisfies:

- • $\nu$ is a measure:

$$ \mathbb{E}\nu(n)=1+o(1). $$

- • $\nu$ satisfies the linear forms condition: Let $m\leqslant k2^{k-1}$ and $t\leqslant 3k-4$ . Let $(L_{ij})_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m,1\leqslant j\leqslant t}$ be a matrix of rational numbers of height $\ll k$ where no row is zero or a rational multiple of another. Let $\psi_{i}:(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{t}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ be linear forms given by $\psi_{i}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{t}L_{ij}x_{j}+b_{i}$ . Then if we consider the natural extension of $\nu$ to $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ , we have that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{x\in(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{t}}(\nu(\psi_{1}(x))\ldots\nu(\psi_{m}(x)))=1+o(1). $$

#### Remark 6.

We would like to note that originally Green and Tao included a correlation condition, but this can be dropped due to the work of Conlon, Fox, and Zhao [3], and Dodos and Kanellopoulos [4].

For such $f$ bounded by pseudorandom measures, we can relate (3) to the Gowers norm of $f$ . In particular, after a technical reduction of rewriting $\Psi$ in $s-$ normal form (which is always possible as described in section 4 of [9]) we can apply the generalized von Neumann theorem:

#### Theorem 3.1 (Green and Tao, Proposition 7.1 [9]).

Let $\nu$ be a $k(s)$ -pseudorandom measure and $f_{1},\ldots,f_{t}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ are functions $|f_{i}(x)|\leqslant\nu(x)$ . If $\Psi$ is a system in $s$ -normal form. If

$$ \min\|f_{j}\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\leqslant\delta, $$

then we have that for some $c>0$ ,

$$ \sum_{n\in[N,2N]^{d}}\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n))\ll_{\Psi,k(s)}\kappa(\delta)N^{d}+o(N^{d}), $$

where $\kappa(\delta)$ is a function that approaches $0$ as $\delta\rightarrow 0.$

#### Proof sketch.

We proceed as in the proof of Proposition 7.1 in [9]; first we take $\varepsilon=\delta^{c}$ in Corollary A.3 (for $c$ yet to be determined) and transfer the problem to $\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z}$ , for $N^{\prime}$ a sufficiently large constant multiple of $N$ . In particular, for $F$ a Lipschitz function of Lipschitz constant $O(\delta^{-c})$ and bounded by $1$ , we want to show that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})^{d}}F(n)\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n))=O(\kappa(\delta)). $$

Next, we expand $F$ under a Fourier expansion: for any $X>1,J=X^{d}$ a Fourier expansion

$$ F(n)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_{j}e(m_{j}n/N^{\prime})+O(\delta^{-c}(\log X)/X) $$

for some coefficients $c_{j}\ll 1$ . We get that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{n\in(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})^{d}} \displaystyle F(n)\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n)) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_{j}\mathbb{E}_{n\in(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})^{d}}e(m_{j}n/N^{\prime})\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n))+O_{k(s)}\left(\frac{\delta^{-c}(\log X)}{X}\right). $$

Here we have applied the linear forms condition for $\nu$ to bound the error term from the Fourier expansion. Let us take $X$ growing slowly in $1/\delta$ .

It is observed by Green and Tao, that the individual exponential sum correlation bounds will be implied by showing

#### Theorem 3.5 ([11, Theorem 1.16]).

Let $G/\Gamma$ be a $m$ -dimensional manifold with a $s$ -step filtration. Let $N\geqslant 1$ and $0\leqslant\delta\leqslant 1/2$ . If ${\mathcal{X}}$ is a $\delta^{-1}$ -rational Mal’cev basis adapted to the filtration and $g\in\mathrm{poly}(\mathbb{Z},G)$ , then at least one of the following is true:

- • $(g(n)\Gamma)$ is $\delta$ -equidistributed in $G/\Gamma$ ,

- • There is a nontrivial horizontal character $\eta:G\rightarrow\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ such that $|\eta|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ and $\|\eta\circ g(n)\|_{C^{\infty}[N]}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 3.4.

Assume $g(Qn+a)$ is not totally- $\delta^{O(1)}$ -equidistributed on $G/\Gamma$ . Then by Theorem 3.5 there is some $q^{\prime}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ and $|\eta|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ such that

$$ \|\eta\circ g(Qq^{\prime}n+a)\|_{C^{\infty}[N]}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}. $$

Let $\psi:G\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ be our map to Mal’cev coordinates (recall that the dimension of $G$ is $m$ ), then we know that $\eta\circ g(n)=k\cdot\psi(g(n))$ for some vector $k\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}$ with $|k|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ . Since $g(n)$ is a polynomial map, we have that

$$ \psi(g(n))=\sum_{j=1}^{d}t_{j}\binom{n}{j}, $$

for some $t_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . Restricting to an arithmetic progression mod $Q$ , we have that

$$ \eta\circ g(Qq^{\prime}n+a)=k\cdot\psi(g(Qq^{\prime}n+a))=\sum_{j=1}^{d}(k\cdot t_{j})\binom{Qq^{\prime}n+a}{j}. $$

We wish to rewrite the above as

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{d}\alpha_{j}\binom{n}{j}, $$

so that we can apply information from the $C^{\infty}[N]$ norm of $\eta\circ g(n)$ . We note that the $C^{\infty}[N]$ is independent of the shift by $a$ , so we can take $a=0$ . We know that $\alpha_{d}=(Qq^{\prime})^{d}(k\cdot t_{d})/d!$ , so we have that

$$ \|(Qq^{\prime})^{d}(k\cdot t_{d})/d!\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll\frac{\delta^{-O(1)}Q^{d}}{N^{d}}. $$

We note that

$$ \alpha_{d-1}=(k\cdot t_{d})(Qq^{\prime})^{d-1}\cdot\frac{d(d-1)}{2d!}(1-Qq^{\prime})+(k\cdot t_{d-1})(Qq^{\prime})^{d-1}\cdot\frac{1}{(d-1)!}. $$

However, since $Q\delta^{-O(1)}/N\ll N^{-1/3}$ we can see the contribution from the terms with $(k\cdot t_{d})$ will be inconsequential to $\|\alpha_{d-1}\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}$ and that

$$ \|(Qq^{\prime})^{d-1}(k\cdot t_{d-1})\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll_{d}\frac{\delta^{-O(1)}Q^{d-1}}{N^{d-1}}. $$

Similarly, we achieve that

$$ \|(Qq^{\prime})^{j}(k\cdot t_{j})\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll_{d}\frac{\delta^{-O(1)}Q^{j}}{N^{j}}, $$

for each $j=1,...,d.$

So, let us pick $u_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ such that $Q^{j}(k\cdot u_{j})\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $|t_{j}-u_{j}|\ll\frac{\delta^{-O(1)}}{N^{j}}$ . We define $\xi(n)$ as the sequence such that

$$ \psi(\xi(n))=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\binom{n}{j}(t_{j}-u_{j}). $$

Next, we pick the vectors $v_{j}$ with denominators of the form $(Qq)^{j}$ with $q\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ and such that $k\cdot u_{j}=k\cdot v_{j}$ . We define $\gamma(n)$ as the sequence such that

$$ \psi(\gamma(n))=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\binom{n}{j}v_{j}. $$

So, we take $g_{1}(n)=\xi^{-1}g\gamma^{-1}(n).$ It is clear via the arguments of [11] that $\xi(n)$ is $(\delta^{-O(1)},N)$ -smooth and $\gamma$ has the correct periodicity properties. So, it remains to construct $g^{\prime}$ totally $\delta^{-O(1)}$ -equidistributed. However, $g_{1}$ is not necessary such; if $g_{1}$ is not totally equidistributed then we can repeat the argument above iteratively, forming $\xi_{1}$ and $\gamma_{1}$ . We note that $\xi(n)\xi_{1}(n)$ will still be $(\delta^{-O(1)},N)$ smooth and $\gamma_{1}(n)\gamma(n)$ periodic. Thus, we repeat the procedure until we have $g^{\prime}(Qn+a)$ totally $\delta^{-O(1)}$ -equidistributed. ∎

First, we note that the contribution of the principal character can be handled by the prime number theorem, so we assume $\chi$ is nonprincipal. For such $\chi$ , we have that

$$ \frac{q}{\varphi(q)}\bigg|\sum_{n\leqslant N}\chi(n)\bigg|\leqslant q\ll M^{1-\eta}. $$

Thus it remains to bound

$$ \sum_{\chi\in\mathcal{S}}\bigg|\sum_{N\leqslant n\leqslant N+M}\Lambda(n)\chi(n)\bigg|. $$

For $T=q^{10}$ , by Perron’s formula (see Proposition 5.25 of [13]), we have

$$ \sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}\Lambda(n)\chi(n)=\sum_{\rho_{\chi}}\frac{(N+M)^{\rho_{\chi}}-N^{\rho_{\chi}}}{\rho_{\chi}}+O\bigg(\frac{N}{T}(\log Nq)^{2}\bigg), $$

where $\rho_{\chi}=\sigma_{\chi}+i\gamma_{\chi}$ runs over nontrivial zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ with $|\gamma_{\chi}|\leqslant T$ . We have

$$ \bigg|\frac{(N+M)^{\rho_{\chi}}-N^{\rho_{\chi}}}{\rho_{\chi}}\bigg|\ll(1+|\gamma_{\chi}|)MN^{\sigma_{\chi}-1}, $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\bigg|\sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}\Lambda(n)\chi(n)\bigg| \displaystyle\ll Mq^{10}\sum_{\chi\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{\rho_{\chi}}N^{\sigma_{\chi}-1} \displaystyle=Mq^{10}\bigg(2N^{-\frac{1}{2}}N(1/2,T)+2\log N\int_{1/2}^{1-\eta}N^{\sigma-1}N(\sigma,T)d\sigma\bigg), $$

where

$$ N(\sigma^{\prime},T)=\#\{\sigma+it:L(\sigma+it,\chi)=0,|t|\leqslant T,\sigma\geqslant\sigma^{\prime}\}. $$

The desired result then follows upon using the log-free zero density estimate

$$ N(\sigma,T)\ll(qT)^{c(1-\sigma)}, $$

where this bound accounts for a possible Siegel zero (as our zero-free region assumed will not in general rule out Siegel zeros). ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 4.1.

First, let us recall that $Q=P(z)$ and write

$$ r=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p>z\\
p^{\ell}||q^{d}\end{subarray}}p^{\ell},\text{ and }R=\frac{(qQ)^{d}}{r}. $$

Observe that both $r|q^{d}$ and $Q|R$ , so we have that for some $\mathcal{P}_{q}\subset{\left\{p|q:p>z\right\}}$

$$ \frac{Q}{\varphi(Q)}=\frac{R}{\varphi(R)}\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{q}}\bigg(1-\frac{1}{p}\bigg)^{-1} $$

Since $z\gg\log Q$ , $\#\mathcal{P}_{q}\ll 1$ , we have that

$$ \prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{q}}\bigg(1-\frac{1}{p}\bigg)^{-1}=1+O{\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)}. $$

By a similar analysis, we obtain that

$$ \frac{Q}{\varphi(Q)}=\frac{R}{\varphi(R)}\bigg(1+O{\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)}\bigg)=\frac{rR}{\varphi(rR)}\bigg(1+O{\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)}\bigg). $$

Therefore, after splitting into residue classes modulo $R$ , it suffices to show that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant N+M\\
n\equiv b(R)\end{subarray}}(\Lambda(n)-R/\varphi(R))F(\gamma(n)\Gamma)\ll\frac{M}{\varphi(R)}(\log Q)^{-\delta} $$

for some $\delta>0$ . By orthogonality and the fact that $(r,R)=1$ , we have that

$$ \displaystyle E \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant N+M\\
n\equiv b(R)\end{subarray}}(\Lambda(n)-R/\varphi(R))F(\gamma(n)\Gamma) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\varphi(R)}\sum_{\chi_{1}(R)}\overline{\chi_{1}}(b)\frac{1}{\varphi(r)}\sum_{\chi_{2}(r)}\overline{\chi_{2}}(R)A(\chi_{2})\sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}(\Lambda(n)-R/\varphi(R))\chi_{1}\chi_{2}(n), $$

where we define

$$ A(\chi_{2})=\sum_{x(r)}\overline{\chi_{2}}(x)F(\gamma(Rx+b)\Gamma). $$

Let $C=\log^{\frac{1}{10}}Q$ . Applying Lemma 4.2, for some $\delta>0$ . the contribution of those $\chi_{2}$ with conductor at least $C$ and not divisible by an odd prime square is

$$ \ll\frac{1}{\varphi(R)\varphi(r)}|A(\chi_{2})|\bigg|\sum_{N\leqslant n\leqslant N+M}(\Lambda(n)-R/\varphi(R))\chi_{1}\chi_{2}(n)\bigg|\ll\frac{M}{\varphi(R)}\frac{r}{\varphi(r)}C^{-\delta}. $$

Let $\mathcal{S}_{\text{ld}}$ be the set of characters $\chi_{1}\chi_{2}$ such that $\chi_{1}\mod R,$ and $\chi_{2}\mod r$ has conductor at most $C$ , or conductor divisible by a square of an odd prime. Then, we have that

$$ E\ll\frac{1}{\varphi(R)\varphi(r)}\sum_{\chi\in\mathcal{S}_{\text{ld}}}\bigg|\sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}(\Lambda(n)-rR/\varphi(rR))\chi(n)\bigg|+\frac{Mr}{\varphi(R)\varphi(r)}C^{-\delta}. $$

Note that since $Q$ is a dutiful modulus and $C=(\log Q)^{1/10}$ (noting that $R|Q^{m}$ for some $m\ll\log q$ ), the desired result follows from Lemma 4.3, where we take $\eta=\frac{1}{(\log X)^{1/10}}$ (in the case that the conductor is divisible by the square of an odd prime, it can not be a quadratic character, and we still have the superior zero-free region as a result).
